name: Jonah
author: The book does not name its writer. Traditionally it is linked to Jonah son of Amittai himself, a prophet from the village of Gath-hepher in Galilee who served in the northern kingdom of Israel under King Jeroboam II, around 780–750 BC. Many scholars think an unknown Israelite writer told Jonah's story much later, perhaps after the Jews returned from exile in Babylon, around 500–400 BC, partly because the story is told about Jonah rather than by him, and because of features of its Hebrew.
audience: On the traditional view, the first hearers were Israelites in the northern kingdom, who knew Assyria as a powerful and brutal empire to the north-east, whose armies had troubled the region before and would soon return. If the book was written later, its readers were Jews rebuilding their life in and around Jerusalem after the exile, under Persian rule and living alongside many other peoples.
era: In Jonah's day the northern kingdom of Israel was enjoying a rare stretch of peace and prosperity under Jeroboam II, regaining land it had lost. To the east lay Assyria, a great empire known for its brutal warfare, and Nineveh, on the River Tigris near modern Mosul in Iraq, was one of its greatest cities. A few decades later, in 722 BC, Assyria would conquer Israel and carry many of its people away.

notes.1:1: Two places come up later in this passage: Joppa was a port on Israel's Mediterranean coast, and Tarshish was a distant trading place far to the west, often linked with southern Spain, the opposite direction from Nineveh.
notes.1:17: Later in this passage, Jonah's prayer is written as a poem in the style of the thanksgiving psalms that Israelites sang at the temple in Jerusalem.
